passage: "Jahnavi, can I ask something?" Rafiq said, walking beside her to school. "Sure." "Why do you always wear a dupatta? Does your family make you?" "Some days it's Amma's rule," Jahnavi said. "Some days it feels like me. Today it just matched my kurta." She grinned. "You're not the first to guess." "Sorry. I assumed." "Everyone does. My cousin wears hers for prayer, my friend Sana never wears one, and neither of us is wrong." "So you can't tell from looking." "Exactly. You'd have to ask, and listen." Rafiq laughed, embarrassed. "Okay. I'm listening. 😅"

qa.q: Who asked Jahnavi about the dupatta?
qa.a: Rafiq asked her, while they were walking to school.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling after Jahnavi answered?
qa.a: He felt a little embarrassed and sorry for assuming, as his apology and laugh show, and probably some curiosity too. 😅

qa.q: How could Rafiq ask about someone's clothing without assuming?
qa.a: He could ask an open, friendly question and really listen, accepting that the same item can be faith, family expectation, choice or style.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when people guess about her dupatta?
qa.a: Somewhat tired of being assumed about, as 'Everyone does' hints, yet she stays friendly and explains patiently.

grounding: A teenager's dupatta can mean family rule, personal feeling or style, so others should ask rather than assume.

passage: After my thread ceremony I thought I'd feel different. Mostly I felt itchy. In the changing room before PE a boy asked if it was some fashion thing. Kalyani, who sits behind me in Bengali class, said, "My uncle wears one to pray, my cousin wears one because his mother insists, and I know a boy who just likes it." She looked at me. "Which are you?" I realised I had no clean answer. Ma wants me to keep it on. Dadu says it has to do with learning, and I like feeling close to him. Some days I tuck it under my shirt, some days I don't. I'm still working it out. - Arnab

qa.q: Where did the boy ask Arnab about the thread?
qa.a: He asked in the changing room before PE.

qa.q: What did Arnab feel when Kalyani asked which he was?
qa.a: He felt uncertain, since he had no clean answer; his reasons seem to mix his mother's wish, closeness to Dadu and his own feeling.

qa.q: How could Arnab reply when someone asks what his thread means?
qa.a: He could share what he knows or say he is still working it out, without needing a tidy answer.

qa.q: What does Kalyani's list of people show?
qa.a: It shows that the same thread can be prayer, family insistence or personal taste, so nobody should assume what it means for someone else.

grounding: A teen wears a sacred thread whose meaning mixes faith, family expectation and choice, and nobody can assume it.

passage:
Teacher's note - Lokesh, Class 10 social science, Monday
During a discussion on choice and culture, one student, meaning well, said Vidya must "have to" wear her hijab. Vidya went quiet, then answered calmly: "Nobody forces me. My mother doesn't even wear one. I chose it in Class 8. It's my faith and, honestly, I like how it looks."
Another student, Parminder, said her own turban was partly faith and partly her grandfather's wish. A third said she wears a bindi for style some days and not others.
I asked the class what they noticed. One boy said, "The same thing can mean different things to different people."
I told them that's exactly why we should ask, not assume. Afterwards the first student apologised to Vidya, and Vidya said, "It's fine. Ask me anything. Just don't tell me what it means for me."

qa.q: When did Vidya choose to wear her hijab?
qa.a: She chose it in Class 8.

qa.q: What might Vidya have felt when told she must "have to" wear it?
qa.a: Vidya probably felt misunderstood and a little hurt, going quiet before calmly explaining it was her own choice.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do to turn the moment into learning?
qa.a: He let students share their own reasons and asked what they noticed, helping the class see that the same item can mean different things.

qa.q: How might the student who apologised have seen the hijab before the discussion?
qa.a: That student seemed to assume it was always imposed, without asking what it meant to Vidya.

grounding: The teacher's note shows that items like a hijab, turban or bindi can be faith, family expectation, choice or style, and that nobody should assume their meaning.

passage:
Thursday
At the swimming pool changing room today, Vishal saw my janeu and said, "Whoa, didn't know you were so religious."
I didn't know what to say. Am I? I wear it because Papa did my thread ceremony last year and Dadaji cried with happiness. I don't pray every day. Some days I forget it's there. Some days I touch it before exams.
So I said, "It's complicated. Family, mostly. And a bit mine."
Vishal nodded. Then he held up his wrist. "This kara is from my friend in Ludhiana. I'm not Sikh. It just means he's my brother."
We looked at each other and laughed. Two bits of thread and metal, and we'd both assumed about the other.
I think I'll keep wearing it. I'll figure out what it means for me later.
- Sachin

qa.q: Who gave Vishal his kara?
qa.a: His friend in Ludhiana.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when Vishal called him religious?
qa.a: Sachin felt caught off guard and unsure, because the janeu's meaning felt mixed, partly family and partly personal.

qa.q: What could both friends learn from the conversation?
qa.a: That an item worn on the body can mean faith, family, friendship or style, so it's better to ask than to assume.

qa.q: How might Sachin's Dadaji see the janeu?
qa.a: Dadaji seems to see it as a deeply happy family and faith moment, which may be different from what it means to Sachin.

grounding: The diary shows a sacred thread and a kara carrying different meanings for their wearers, and friends learning not to assume.

passage: In the kasba's government school, the cricket nets were just a torn fishing net strung between two neem trees. Yash had stripped to his vest for batting practice, and the white thread across his shoulder showed. Rinku, new from the city, pointed. "Your parents make you wear that? Mine never would." Yash tapped it. "Nobody makes me. I asked for the ceremony. My grandfather tied it." He shrugged. "Some days it's prayer. Some days I forget it's there." Imran, padding up, grinned. "Don't look at me next. Yes, it's a cap. On Fridays I wear it for namaz. Other days it's because Abba says the sun will fry my brain." Rinku laughed, then went red. "Sorry. I thought it all meant the same thing for everyone." "Ask," said Yash, "and we'll tell you." Imran tossed Rinku the ball. "Now bowl. That's the only tradition here."

qa.q: Who tied Yash's thread?
qa.a: His grandfather tied it.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Rinku asked if his parents made him wear it?
qa.a: Yash seemed calm and a little amused, maybe slightly defensive since he said nobody makes him; the thread carries mixed meanings for him, prayer some days and habit on others.

qa.q: What is a better way for Rinku to handle this next time?
qa.a: Ask what the item means to that person instead of guessing, as Yash suggested, since the same thread or cap can mean faith, family or habit.

qa.q: How did Rinku see the thread at first?
qa.a: Rinku assumed it was something parents force on children, and went red on realising it meant different things to different people.

grounding: It shows a sacred thread and a cap carrying faith, family and everyday meanings for different teenagers, and a newcomer learning not to assume.
